claims.text: Structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoparticles from 473 to 1923 K is governed by a balance between entropy stabilization and atomic-diffusion kinetics.
Similar constituent atomic sizes and high diffusion activation barriers allow configurational entropy to kinetically trap the solid solution.
Kinetic trapping prevents phase segregation.
Large differences in atomic radii or diffusion kinetics promote elemental segregation or intermetallic formation at elevated temperature.
Nanoparticles containing five or more metals can initially crystallize as homogeneous single-phase solid solutions.
Using an inert or reducing atmosphere minimizes extraneous oxidation during thermal exposure.
Lattice strain arising from atomic-size mismatch modulates atomic-diffusion kinetics.
Diffusion kinetics governed by lattice strain determine the onset of segregation or intermetallic formation.
At moderate temperatures, high configurational entropy stabilizes the solid solution.
As temperature increases, differences in diffusion activation energies and lattice strain become critical to phase stability.
An element with a lower diffusion barrier can diffuse faster and induce local segregation or ordering.
Local segregation or ordering disrupts structural and chemical integrity.
Nanoparticles with narrowly matched atomic sizes have correspondingly high diffusion barriers.
Nanoparticles with narrowly matched atomic sizes and high diffusion barriers will retain a homogeneous solid solution throughout 473–1923 K.
Retention of a homogeneous solid solution will produce consistent catalytic and thermoelectric performance throughout 473–1923 K.
Nanoparticles with larger disparities in atomic size and diffusion properties will exhibit phase separation.
Phase separation will cause deterioration of catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
Closely matched atomic radii imply similar diffusion activation energies.
Oxidizing or strongly reducing environments may independently alter stability through surface oxidation or reduction.

Opposite comparative behavior—segregation and degradation in the matched-size set but homogeneity and stable performance in the mismatched-size set—would falsify the proposed control by diffusion kinetics and lattice strain.
